# Writing Guidelines

## Know Your Audience

- **Primary audience:** the program committee / selection reviewers
- They're experts who've seen hundreds of submissions
- You have ~30 seconds to grab their interest
- They sort into an "A pile" (excited to read) and a "B pile" (chore to read)

## Keep It Short and Clear

- Short abstracts get into the "A pile"
- Resist the temptation to argue for your conclusion in the abstract
- Let the abstract create intrigue — make them want to hear the full talk
- Don't cram everything about the topic into the abstract

## Abstract Checklist

- [ ] Follows the four-sentence structure (or close to it)
- [ ] Has one clear, startling sentence/claim
- [ ] Written for experts who need to be intrigued quickly
- [ ] Short and scannable (not a wall of text)
- [ ] Makes the reader want to know "how can they say that?"
- [ ] Clear benefit/takeaway for attendees
- [ ] Avoids jargon that only you understand
- [ ] Problem is relatable and important

## Common Mistakes to Avoid

- **"The Foo System In All Its Glory"** — trying to include everything instead of focusing on one hook
- **Vague claims** — "this talk will be interesting" vs. specific value
- **Arguing in the abstract** — save the proof for the talk itself
- **Writing to the general audience first** — get past the committee first
- **Playing it safe** — boring, hedged statements don't grab attention

## Refinement Process

When refining an existing abstract:

1. Identify the startling sentence — if you can't find one, that's the problem
2. Check the four-sentence structure — is anything missing?
3. Cut ruthlessly — every word should earn its place
4. Read it as a tired reviewer — does it make you want to learn more?
